chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Ahmad ibn Idris narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad, from Yusuf ibn al-Harith, from Abdullah ibn Yazid, from Hayya ibn Sharih, who said: Salim ibn Ghaylan narrated to us, from al-Darraj, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'd al-Khudri, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family)
He said: 'I seek refuge in God from disbelief and debt.' It was said: 'O Messenger of God, does debt equal disbelief?' He (peace be upon him and his family) replied: 'Yes.'

key_terms.يَعْدِلُ: To be equal to / to equate

ai.seo_question: Why does the Prophet consider debt to be equal to disbelief?
ai.summary: In this hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) seeks refuge from *al-dayn* (debt), which scholars interpret not merely as financial obligation but as a spiritual burden that can distract from devotion or lead to *kufr* (disbelief) if one breaks promises to satisfy creditors. This comparison underscores the gravity of debt in Shia jurisprudence, where it is often viewed as a 'shameful' state that impedes spiritual clarity and social integrity. The affirmation highlights how material encumbrances can have profound theological consequences, linking financial responsibility directly to one's standing before God.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 2-39 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Ahmad ibn Idris quoted on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Yusuf ibn al-Harith, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Yazid, on the authority of Hayat ibn Sharih, on the authority of Salim ibn Qayla, on the authority of Dur’raj, on the authority of Abil Haysam, on the authority of Abi Sa’ad al-Khidry, “I heard God’s Prophet (MGB) say,
‘I Seek refuge in God from disbelief and debt.’ He (MGB) was told, ‘O Prophet of God! Is debt equal to disbelief?’ He (MGB) replied, ‘Yes.’”
